title: After the USAID cuts, where did 50,000 development workers go?
excerpt: Up to 50,000 development jobs have gone since the 2025 aid cuts. There is still no official count, and Devlens found no scheme from government, donors or NGO networks to help the people who lost them.

image.alt: Graphic illustration by Devlens: rows of small figures in dark grey, a scattered few highlighted in green

content:
DEVLENS SPECIAL · Analysis · Workforce · 7 November 2026

Twenty-one months after the aid cuts began, Bangladesh's development workforce has not recovered. It has been rebuilt on shorter contracts, lower ranks and smaller grants, nobody has counted who was lost, and Devlens found no one helping them.

On the night of 31 January 2025, more than 1,000 staff at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) received termination letters. It was the first large wave of job losses after a US stop-work order halted USAID-funded projects in Bangladesh. Over the following months, 55 of the 59 USAID projects running in the country closed, according to the Association of Unemployed Development Professionals (AUDP).

Estimates of how many development jobs went since then range from 20,000 to more than 50,000. In March 2025 the NGO Affairs Bureau said it was preparing a brief on the impact for the government, but no figure has been made public.

Devlens reviewed public records, agency announcements and reporting from Dhaka and Cox's Bazar to trace what happened to this workforce. The picture is of a sector that shrank, then reorganised itself in ways that leave the people who stayed less secure.

Key findings

  • No one knows the true number. Published estimates of lost jobs differ by 30,000, and each comes from sector groups rather than official data.
  • No one is helping them. Devlens found no government scheme, donor fund or NGO network programme for laid-off development workers. Their own association's appeals have gone unanswered.
  • The cuts went beyond USAID. UNICEF ended contracts for 1,179 host community teachers in the Rohingya camps, UNHCR cut about 3,500 posts worldwide, and UK aid to Bangladesh is being halved.
  • Senior roles vanished fastest. Global postings for project director and chief of party jobs fell from 630 to 105 in a year, according to Devex. Former managers report being rehired at lower grades.
  • Contracts became consultancies. Surviving NGOs are replacing permanent staff with consultants paid per deliverable, carrying no liability when funding ends.
  • Big organisations moved down-market. Organisations that once ignored projects under $2 million now compete for $100,000 grants, squeezing out local NGOs.

How many jobs were lost

The 50,000 figure that dominates the debate comes from AUDP, a platform of laid-off development workers. At a press conference in May 2025, its convenor Zinat Ara Afroze said more than 50,000 people could lose their jobs by August, including about 10,000 core NGO staff already let go and field-level officers. Other estimates are far lower.

The gap matters. A range of 20,000 to 50,000 is too wide for anyone to plan retraining, tax relief or job placement. Afroze herself has called for an official survey of the workers who lost jobs and an economic impact assessment, writing in The Daily Star in June 2025.

Who was hit

The first wave came from USAID. icddr,b, one of the country's best-known research bodies, issued more than 1,000 termination letters within days of the stop-work order. Around 240 Bangladeshi NGOs ran projects through USAID's main implementing partners, and 327 NGOs in total had USAID funding affected, according to a survey reported by The Daily Star in February 2025.

The second wave hit the Rohingya response. In June 2025 UNICEF ended the contracts of 1,179 Bangladeshi teachers who taught Rohingya children in camp learning centres, calling it "a funding-driven decision". UNHCR cut about 3,500 posts worldwide the same month, reducing staffing costs by 30%. Humanitarian workers in Cox's Bazar describe posts left unfilled, larger caseloads and less secure contracts, according to an analysis published by the Humanitarian Practice Network in May 2026.

The third wave is still arriving. UK bilateral aid to Bangladesh falls from £66.7 million in 2025-26 to £31 million in 2026-27, and a UK-funded Practical Action climate project in the Sundarbans closed two years early in June. The Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) now counts about 2,200 small and medium NGOs at risk of a funding crunch.

International contractors left altogether. Chemonics International and Tetra Tech shut their Bangladesh offices, and ACDI/VOCA declared dissolution, The Business Standard reported in May 2026.

The new job market

The jobs that came back are not the jobs that were lost. Four changes stand out.

Fewer senior posts. Globally, postings on the Devex jobs platform fell about 25% in a year, and project director and chief of party roles dropped from 630 to 105. Salaries fell for most roles, and new postings skewed towards junior positions and short-term contracts. In Bangladesh, a programme manager at an international NGO told The Business Standard he found work after five months, at the same organisation, demoted to senior officer. Tony Michel Gomes, former director of communications at CARE Bangladesh, put it plainly: "The higher your position was, the harder it became to find a new job."

Consultancies instead of contracts. NGOs that survived are bringing in programme officers and field coordinators project by project, paid per deliverable. The work gets done, but institutional knowledge no longer builds up inside organisations, and workers carry the risk when funding ends.

Big players chasing small grants. Large organisations that once ignored projects under $2 million are now "aggressively competing for $100,000 projects just to survive", development professional Syed Aminur Rahman told The Business Standard. That squeezes the local NGOs that relied on those smaller grants.

Localisation helps some, not most. Donors cutting overall aid increasingly want money to go to local organisations directly. That favours national NGOs with track records and compliance systems, not the small community groups that employ field staff in districts such as Satkhira and Khulna.

The wider economy offers little cover. Bdjobs, the country's largest jobs site, called the market "largely stagnant" in late 2025, and private-sector credit growth hit a four-year low of 6.23% in October 2025.

Where people went

There is no data on where laid-off development workers ended up. The accounts published so far, mostly in The Business Standard and The Daily Star, point to five paths.

  1. Back into the sector, lower down. Some rejoined their old employer or a peer at a lower grade, often on short project contracts. Several moved to Cox's Bazar, where the Rohingya response still hires, though on contracts that can end within months.
  2. Freelance consulting. Specialists in gender, monitoring and evaluation, and communications have turned to consultancy. Senior former USAID project managers have approached small local NGOs for consultancy work, one NGO chief executive in Khulna said.
  3. Small business. A former accounts officer used his savings to import clothing, in a market already saturated.
  4. Still searching. A former communications lead was still unemployed ten months after her project shut. Afroze reported more than 20 applications without a single reply.
  5. Leaving. Some are looking abroad. A former gender specialist told The Business Standard that leaving the country now seems the most realistic option.

The private sector has struggled to absorb them. Employers often do not know how to use development skills, and NGO experience can count against applicants, according to workers interviewed by The Business Standard. AUDP now runs an online forum where members share vacancies and support each other.

Is anyone helping?

Almost two years after the first termination letters, Devlens found no government scheme, donor fund or sector-wide programme aimed at Bangladesh's laid-off development workers. Most of them were on project contracts that ended without severance, according to NGO Affairs Bureau figures reported by BBC Bangla in early 2025.

Government. The only official step on record came in March 2025, when the NGO Affairs Bureau asked NGOs to absorb jobless staff into other projects "as much as they can". In July 2025 AUDP wrote to the bureau's director general asking for an inter-ministerial committee on re-employment and an economic impact assessment. By November it had received no reply, the Daily Times of Bangladesh reported. Devlens found no measure for these workers from either the interim government or its elected successor.

The wider jobs push does not target them. The Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) raised its financing target for FY2026-27 by 45% to Tk 160 billion to create jobs. That money goes to microenterprises, youth, women and marginalised communities, not to displaced professionals.

NGO networks. The Association of Development Agencies in Bangladesh (ADAB) estimated that about 300 projects had closed and more than 100 NGOs were directly affected, but has announced no support scheme for staff. Its president's own organisation, HEED Bangladesh, faced a 30% budget cut and expected to cut its workforce by a similar share. Recommendations from the Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE) focus on helping NGOs diversify their funding, not on the people who lost jobs.

Donors and the UN. Devlens found no public record of a donor or UN transition fund for national staff in Bangladesh, including from agencies that cut posts here.

Help abroad rarely reaches Dhaka. In the United States, former USAID staff can turn to dozens of networks offering counselling, coaching, job boards and business support. Devex listed more than 20 in December 2025. Almost all are built around American federal workers, and none is designed for locally employed staff in countries such as Bangladesh.

Workers helping themselves. In practice, the main support is AUDP itself: a volunteer platform that shares vacancies, runs an online forum and lobbies on members' behalf. A Times of Bangladesh survey of laid-off development workers, published in November 2025, found about 69% still unemployed, four in five of them with more than ten years' experience. The survey's sample size was not published.

What has been proposed

Devlens found no public record that any of these proposals has been adopted.

Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury told the BIDS seminar in October that NGOs should take a bigger part in delivering government programmes. If that happens, it could create the first new stream of jobs for the sector since the cuts. It would also tie NGO employment more closely to state budgets.

Count us in: the Devlens workforce survey

Because no one has counted, Devlens is asking. We are preparing an anonymous survey for anyone who has worked in Bangladesh's development or humanitarian sector since January 2024, whether you lost your job, kept it or changed roles. It takes about five minutes. We will publish the results as a follow-up Devlens Special, with no individual or organisation identified.

The survey asks:

  1. Were you working in the development or humanitarian sector in January 2025? What type of employer (UN agency, international NGO, national NGO, local NGO, research body, contractor)?
  2. Was your job affected by funding cuts since January 2025 (lost, shortened, downgraded, unaffected)?
  3. Which donor funded your project, if you know?
  4. What is your situation today (same job, new sector job, consultancy, other sector, own business, abroad, unemployed)?
  5. How many months did it take to find new work, if you did?
  6. How does your current monthly income compare with January 2025 (higher, about the same, up to 25% lower, 25 to 50% lower, more than 50% lower)?
  7. Are you on a permanent contract, fixed-term contract or consultancy?
  8. Your role level and years of experience
  9. Your district and gender (optional)
  10. Are you planning to leave the sector or the country in the next 12 months?
  11. What one support would help most (job matching, reskilling, tax relief, startup funding, other)?

Take part: the online form will be linked here. To be told when it opens, or to share anonymised staffing data from your organisation, email devlensbangladesh@gmail.com.

About this analysis

This Devlens Special draws on agency announcements from icddr,b, UNICEF and UNHCR; statements and proposals by the Association of Unemployed Development Professionals; the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies study of NGO financing presented on 6 October 2026; UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office allocations; Devex jobs platform data; and workers' accounts published in Bangladeshi media. No official count of development-sector job losses in Bangladesh exists, so all job-loss figures here are estimates and are attributed to the organisations that made them. All graphics are by Devlens Bangladesh.
